# Before you start

This tutorial follows the presentation's BT, BT--SBM and PL practicals. Each
practical comes after the corresponding model's theory session. The tutorial
and presentation contain separate copies of the same analysis code, with
matching chunk labels and seeds. Neither file reads code from the other.

For downloads and a complete setup guide, including the working directory,
start at the [website Tutorial page](https://lapo-santi.github.io/RBBayes/tutorial.html).

Run the chunks in order in RStudio, or use *Knit* to generate the complete
HTML document. Matching R/package versions and optional packages are needed
for matching Monte Carlo results. Plot dimensions differ between the two
formats. Runtime depends on the computer.

**Installation (run once).** The code below installs the GitHub development
version while the package is being prepared for CRAN. Building its C++ code
from source requires standard R build tools. If these are not already installed:

> **Windows:** install the [Rtools version matching your R version](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/), then restart RStudio.
>
> **macOS:** run `xcode-select --install` in **Terminal**, then complete the installation dialogue. The [Xcode Command Line Tools](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/installing-the-command-line-tools/) are sufficient; the full Xcode application is not required.
>
> These tools are needed for the source installation below. An available CRAN binary normally does not require compiling the package yourself.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("remotes", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
remotes::install_github("lapo-santi/RBBayes")

# Optional: coda and bayesplot enable their sections; salso enables its
# partition search (a built-in search is used when salso is absent).
install.packages(c("coda", "bayesplot", "salso"))
```

## Where to find this tutorial after installation

Package installation stores the tutorial in the `tutorial` folder **inside
the installed RBBayes package**, alongside its other resources. It does not
create a Desktop file or automatically open an RStudio tab. The exact package
library location depends on the computer; use `system.file()` to find it.
This hands-on tutorial is a bundled file, so it is not listed by `vignette()`.

**Read the finished tutorial in a browser:**

```{r tutorial-read, eval = FALSE}
browseURL(system.file("tutorial", "RBBayes-tutorial.html",
                      package = "RBBayes", mustWork = TRUE))
```

**Copy the editable source into your current project and open it:**

```{r tutorial-path, eval = FALSE}
tutorial_source <- system.file("tutorial", "RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd",
                               package = "RBBayes", mustWork = TRUE)
if (!file.exists("RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd")) {
  stopifnot(file.copy(tutorial_source, "RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd"))
}
file.edit("RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd")
```

The copy appears in the folder returned by `getwd()` and should open in
RStudio's Source pane. The code preserves an existing file of that name;
choose a new project folder if you need a fresh copy without replacing your
work. Running these commands is a separate step after installing the package.

```{r packages}
library(RBBayes)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
has_coda <- requireNamespace("coda", quietly = TRUE)
has_bayesplot <- requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE)
packageVersion("RBBayes")
```

**What you will do.**

1. **BT:** simulate comparisons with one distinct generating strength per
   player; prepare the edge list, fit the model, interpret normalised
   strengths and assess the MCMC.
2. **BT--SBM:** generate a new example with shared block strengths only after
   introducing the block model, then estimate its partition and uncertainty.
   Apply the same block-model workflow to the real 2017 ATP season.
3. **PL:** prepare rankings and fit a Plackett--Luce model.

The BT and BT--SBM simulations are different datasets. Their summaries
illustrate each model's features rather than compare models on identical
observations.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $n$; $i, j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ | number of items (players); item indices |
| $y_{ij}$ | number of wins of $i$ over $j$ |
| $n_{ij} = y_{ij} + y_{ji}$ | number of comparisons between $i$ and $j$ |
| $\lambda_i > 0$ | strength of item $i$ in the standard BT model |

The BT model says
$$
y_{ij} \mid \lambda \sim \operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(n_{ij}, \frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_i + \lambda_j}\right),
\qquad i < j.
$$
Counts for distinct unordered pairs are conditionally independent given the
strengths. We use one direction per pair because $y_{ji}=n_{ij}-y_{ij}$.

# BT practical: individual player strengths

This practical follows the BT theory session. We start with twenty fictional
players with distinct generating strengths, without introducing blocks.
The model receives an independent Gamma prior for each strength; specify
`shape_lambda` and leave the rate at its package default.

## Simulate and prepare the comparisons

```{r simulate}
lambda <- exp(seq(log(12), 0, length.out = 20)) # One strength per player.
edges <- simulate_data(
  model = "bt", latent_strength = lambda,
  item_labels = paste("Player", seq_along(lambda)),
  matches_per_pair = 20, seed = 101, format = "edgelist"
)
edges |> slice_head(n = 6) |> knitr::kable()
```

`simulate_data(model = "bt")` takes one positive generating strength
$\lambda_i$ per player. For each unordered pair $i<j$, it draws
$y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_{ij},\lambda_i/(\lambda_i+\lambda_j))$
and sets $y_{ji}=n_{ij}-y_{ij}$. Here every pair plays twenty matches.
The strengths are supplied by us, rather than drawn from the fitting prior.
The output order is shuffled reproducibly using `seed`.

`format = "edgelist"` returns aggregated `winner`, `loser`, `count` rows,
including both directions and zero counts. The default `format = "data"`
returns validated pairwise data directly; `"matrix"` returns a win-count
matrix. Real observations use the same preparation interface:

```{r as-bt-data}
tennis <- as_bt_data(edges, format = "edgelist")
tennis
```

For `as_bt_data()`, `format = "edgelist"` reads the standard `count` column.
Use `format = "matches"` when each row is one match outcome, or
`format = "matrix"` for a square win-count matrix. Repeated directed edges
are added and self-comparisons are rejected. The earlier explicit
`count = "count"` interface remains supported, but is not needed here.

## Explore the data first

Before fitting anything, look at the raw outcomes.

```{r eda-table}
# Each edge contributes wins to its winner and losses to its loser.
player_table <- bind_rows(
  edges |> transmute(player = winner, matches = count, wins = count),
  edges |> transmute(player = loser, matches = count, wins = 0)
) |>
  group_by(player) |>
  summarise(across(c(matches, wins), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(win_rate = wins / matches) |>
  arrange(desc(win_rate))

player_table |> slice_head(n = 6) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r eda-winrate, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(player_table, aes(x = win_rate, y = reorder(player, win_rate))) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Overall win rate", y = NULL,
       title = "Overall win rate of each player") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Win rates provide a descriptive ordering before any model is fitted. Here
the generating strengths are individual values, so we do not interpret gaps
as evidence of generating blocks.

```{r eda-matrix, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_pairwise_outcomes(tennis, reorder = FALSE)
```

With `reorder = FALSE`, both axes retain the input item order.

This illustrates R's S3 object-oriented interface. `tennis` has class
`btsbm_pairwise_data`. The generic `plot_pairwise_outcomes()` selects its
method for that class. A class identifies a kind of object; its methods
implement operations on that kind of object. The corresponding BT-fit method
extracts the observed data from a fitted model. Both methods plot observed
counts, not fitted probabilities.

```{r eda-matrix-ordered, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_pairwise_outcomes(tennis, reorder = TRUE)
```

With `reorder = TRUE`, both axes are sorted by decreasing observed overall
win rate. This uses the observations alone; it does not estimate model
strengths or a partition.

## The standard Bradley--Terry model

Each player gets their own strength $\lambda_i$ with an independent Gamma
prior. We specify only `shape_lambda`; the constructor supplies the common
rate automatically; omitting its
argument does not remove the rate from the Gamma distribution.

```{r fit-bt}
bt_fit <- fit_model(
  tennis,
  bt_model(shape_lambda = 2),
  mcmc_control(iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 12)
)
bt_fit
summary(bt_fit)
```

`iter` counts all iterations; `warmup` specifies the **burn-in** to discard.
Thus this run retains 2,000 of its 4,000 iterations. The R argument is still
called `warmup`, and the package's printed summary calls it warm-up.

### Relative strengths

The likelihood identifies strength ratios: multiplying every $\lambda_i$ by
the same positive constant changes no win probability. A proper Gamma prior
supplies the posterior raw scale, which the likelihood itself does not identify.

For retained draw $s$, the package reports the normalised share
$$
q_i^{(s)}=\frac{\lambda_i^{(s)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_j^{(s)}}.
$$
If $S$ is the number of retained draws, the plotted dot is
$\bar q_i=S^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{S}q_i^{(s)}$, an estimate of $E(q_i\mid y)$.
Normalise **each draw before averaging**; this is generally different from
normalising the vector of raw posterior means.

Shares sum to one in every draw, so posterior mean shares also sum to one.
Their average **across players** is always $1/n$ (0.05 for twenty players),
although individual posterior means differ. The dashed line marks that
reference, not each player's posterior mean.

```{r bt-strength, fig.height = 6}
bt_strength <- strength_summary(bt_fit)
plot_strength_summary(bt_fit)
```

```{r bt-ranks, fig.height = 6}
plot_rank_intervals(bt_fit)
```

Rank 1 is strongest. The rank plot uses 95% central intervals by default;
`plot_strength_summary()` above uses 90%. In a block model tied strengths
receive average ranks (midranks).

### Who is stronger than whom? $\Pr(\lambda_i > \lambda_j \mid y)$

Rankings hide how sure we are about each comparison. `prob_stronger()` returns,
for every pair, the posterior probability that the row player is stronger than
the column player.

```{r bt-prob-stronger, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 8.5}
plot_prob_stronger(bt_fit)
```

The colour scale is centred at 0.5. White indicates little posterior preference
for either strength ordering. Under the standard BT model, exact strength ties
have posterior probability zero. Sampling variation still makes the ordering
uncertain.

This is a probability of **strength ordering**, not a posterior predictive
win probability. The latter averages $\lambda_i/(\lambda_i+\lambda_j)$ over
the posterior draws.

### Checking the MCMC

Convergence checks use the normalised strength shares. Exported columns are
named after the players, such as `rel_strength[Player 1]`.

```{r bt-coda, eval = has_coda}
top_players <- strength_summary(bt_fit) |>
  slice_head(n = 4) |>
  transmute(parameter = paste0("rel_strength[", item, "]")) |>
  pull(parameter)
chain <- coda::as.mcmc(bt_fit)
round(coda::effectiveSize(chain)[top_players])
```

ESS is interpreted relative to the `r bt_fit$control$iter - bt_fit$control$warmup`
retained draws. Autocorrelation reduces information; inspect traces too.
The [bayesplot appendix](#appendix-bayesplot) gives trace and interval examples.

A single chain cannot reveal every problem. Run a second, independent chain
with a different seed and compare:

```{r bt-two-chains, eval = has_coda}
bt_fit2 <- fit_model(tennis, bt_fit$model,
                     mcmc_control(iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 112))
chains <- as_mcmc_chains(list(bt_fit, bt_fit2))
coda::gelman.diag(chains[, top_players], autoburnin = FALSE, multivariate = FALSE)
```

Values of the potential scale reduction factor close to 1 are reassuring,
but are not proof of convergence. `autoburnin = FALSE` prevents coda from
discarding a second burn-in. We use `multivariate = FALSE` because the full
vector of normalised strengths sums to one and has singular covariance.
These short teaching runs need longer, independently checked chains for a
substantive analysis.

# BT--SBM practical: shared block strengths

The BT--SBM introduces the following quantities:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $K$ | number of occupied item blocks |
| $z_i \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ | block membership of player $i$ |
| $\lambda_k > 0$ | strength shared by players in block $k$ |
| $\theta_i=\lambda_{z_i}$ | implied strength of player $i$ |

Given the partition, occupied-block strengths have independent
Gamma priors with shape `shape_lambda` and the package-default rate. The partition $z$ receives a
prior under which $K$ is random. The win probability is
$\theta_i/(\theta_i+\theta_j)$, so same-block players beat each other with
probability 1/2. Block membership does not depend on the numerical labels
used to encode the partition.

## Generate a block-model example

We now create a **new** dataset whose players share strengths within generating
blocks. This comes after the BT--SBM theory session and its notation above.

```{r simulate-sbm}
edges_sbm <- simulate_data(
  model = "bt-sbm",
  n_blocks = 4, latent_strength = c(12, 6, 2, 1), # One strength per block.
  players_per_block = 5, # Unequal sizes are also allowed: c(3, 4, 5, 8).
  matches_per_pair = 20, seed = 101, format = "edgelist"
)
tennis_sbm <- as_bt_data(edges_sbm, format = "edgelist")
truth <- attr(edges_sbm, "truth")
edges_sbm |> slice_head(n = 6) |> knitr::kable()
```

`model = "bt-sbm"` interprets `latent_strength` as one positive value per block.
A scalar `players_per_block = 5` gives five players in every block. Unequal
sizes are allowed: `players_per_block = c(3, 4, 5, 8)` gives those four sizes,
with twenty players in total. If omitted, `n_blocks` is inferred from the
number of generating strengths. The function randomly assigns memberships to
player names subject to these sizes, then simulates all pair counts using
the implied player strengths $\theta_i=\lambda_{z_i}$.

The `truth` attribute records the generating blocks and strengths. We use it
to assess recovery; it is not supplied to `fit_model()`.

### Prior on the number of blocks

Before seeing data, how many blocks does each partition prior expect among
$n = 20$ players?

```{r prior-K}
priors <- list(
  Gnedin = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5),
  DP = dirichlet_process_prior(concentration = 1),
  PitmanYor = pitman_yor_prior(concentration = 1, discount = 0.2),
  DirMult_max4 = dirichlet_multinomial_prior(max_clusters = 4, concentration = 1)
)
tibble(
  prior = names(priors),
  mean_K = vapply(priors, function(p) prior_mean_K(20, p), numeric(1)),
  sd_K = sqrt(vapply(priors, function(p) prior_variance_K(20, p), numeric(1)))
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2) # NA: variance not implemented for PY/DM.
```

For fixed $n$, $K$ is always at most $n$. The Gnedin prior also allows a
random, almost surely finite limiting number of blocks as the number of
items grows; it has no fixed upper bound. With the chosen hyperparameter,
its prior mean and standard deviation for $n=20$ are about 3.99 and 5.10.
A wide prior is still informative: examine sensitivity to its hyperparameter.
For the Dirichlet--multinomial, `max_clusters = 4` fixes an upper bound, and
`concentration = 1` is the symmetric concentration **per** possible block.
The DP and Pitman--Yor priors have no fixed finite bound as $n$ grows.

### Fit

```{r fit-sbm}
sbm_model <- bt_sbm_model(
  shape_lambda = 2,
  item_clustering = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5)
)
sbm_model
sbm_fit <- fit_model(tennis_sbm, sbm_model,
                     mcmc_control(iter = 10000, warmup = 5000, seed = 2))
summary(sbm_fit)
```

`summary()` reports the number of blocks and an estimated partition for a
block model. Player-level implied strengths remain well defined, so
`strength_summary(sbm_fit)` and `as.matrix(sbm_fit)` are also available;
they do not require matching arbitrary block labels between draws.

### How many blocks?

```{r K-table}
posterior_K_table(sbm_fit)
```

The generating value is $K=4$. It receives
`r round(100 * mean(sbm_fit$draws$n_item_clusters == 4), 1)`% of the retained
draws, while `r round(100 * mean(sbm_fit$draws$n_item_clusters > 4), 1)`% have
more than four blocks. These are Monte Carlo estimates under the specified
likelihood and priors.

```{r K-trace, fig.height = 3}
plot_mcmc_traces(sbm_fit)
```

### The estimated partition and the reordered data

`partition_point_estimate()` searches for a partition with low posterior
expected variation of information (VI) loss. It uses `salso` when installed,
otherwise a built-in candidate search; neither guarantees a global minimum.
The built-in VI search evaluates a shortlist against at most 1,000 evenly
spaced retained draws. The centre may therefore depend on the search method.
Blocks are labelled in decreasing order of the average posterior mean
normalised player strength within the estimated block. Compare with the truth:

```{r z-hat}
set.seed(100)
z_hat <- partition_point_estimate(sbm_fit)
tibble(item = names(z_hat), estimated_block = unname(z_hat)) |>
  left_join(truth, by = "item") |>
  count(estimated_block, true_block) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = true_block, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Now redraw the outcome matrix with players ordered by their estimated block:

```{r ordered-adjacency, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_ordered_adjacency(sbm_fit, z_hat = z_hat, clean_fun = NULL)
```

This plot uses the new BT--SBM dataset and orders its observations by the
estimated partition. That ordering uses a fitted model, unlike the observed
win-rate ordering used in the BT practical.

### Membership probabilities

`plot_assignment_probabilities()` shows, for each player, the posterior
probability of belonging to each block, **conditional on a given number of
blocks** $K$. In each retained draw the function relabels blocks in decreasing
strength order, so column 1 means the strongest block in that draw, not an
unchanging group of players. This ordering is needed even when $K$ is fixed.
The colour scale is centred at 0.5: blue means "more likely than not".

```{r assign-K4, fig.height = 6}
plot_assignment_probabilities(sbm_fit, k_show = 4, clean_fun = NULL)
# Check recovery without depending on the arbitrary numerical block labels.
true_tier <- truth$true_block[match(tennis_sbm$item_labels, truth$item)]
true_pairs <- outer(true_tier, true_tier, `==`)
recovers_truth <- apply(sbm_fit$draws$item_cluster, 1, function(z) {
  all(outer(z, z, `==`) == true_pairs)
})
recovery_given_K4 <- mean(recovers_truth[sbm_fit$draws$n_item_clusters == 4])
```

Among the `r sum(sbm_fit$draws$n_item_clusters == 4)` retained draws with
$K=4$, `r round(100 * recovery_given_K4, 1)`% reproduce the generating partition.
This does **not** imply posterior certainty: the
`r round(100 * mean(sbm_fit$draws$n_item_clusters != 4), 1)`% of draws with a
different $K$ are excluded. Nor does a sampled frequency of zero establish
zero posterior probability. Now inspect draws with five blocks:

```{r assign-K5, fig.height = 6}
plot_assignment_probabilities(sbm_fit, k_show = 5, clean_fun = NULL)
```

In this run the five-block draws split one generating tier into two
sub-blocks. Since columns refer to strength order, splitting a strong tier
can shift the column labels of weaker, otherwise unchanged tiers. Intermediate
cells can therefore reflect both splitting and changes in block order; the
label-invariant summaries below separate these effects.

### Which players belong together?

The posterior similarity matrix does not condition on $K$: cell $(i, j)$ is
$\Pr(z_i = z_j \mid y)$, the proportion of all draws in which the two players
share a block. Outlines show the estimated partition.

```{r psm, fig.height = 7.5, fig.width = 8.5}
set.seed(100)  # Use the same partition search as in z-hat for the outlines.
plot_posterior_similarity(sbm_fit)
similarity <- posterior_similarity(sbm_fit)
within_estimate <- outer(z_hat, z_hat, `==`)
within_similarity <- range(similarity[within_estimate & row(similarity) != col(similarity)])
outside_similarity <- range(similarity[!within_estimate])
```

Off-diagonal co-clustering frequencies within estimated blocks range from
`r round(within_similarity[1], 3)` to `r round(within_similarity[2], 3)`;
between estimated blocks they range from `r round(outside_similarity[1], 3)`
to `r round(outside_similarity[2], 3)`. `block_stability()` checks whether
separation comes from splitting a block, merging with outside players, or both:

```{r block-stability}
sbm_stability <- block_stability(sbm_fit, z_hat)
sbm_stability[, c("block", "size", "together", "split", "merged")]
```

The largest sampled `merged` frequency is `r max(sbm_stability$merged)`.
In this run no retained draw joins players from different estimated blocks;
the observed uncertainty concerns splits. This is a property of these draws,
not a proof that posterior merging probability is zero.

`together` means the whole estimated block is reproduced exactly: all its
players are together and no outside player joins. `split` and `merged` can
both occur in one draw, so the three columns need not sum to one.

### Credible ball for the partition

Following [Wade and Ghahramani (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1214/17-BA1073),
we choose the smallest VI radius around the estimated partition $\hat z$
that contains **at least** 95% of retained draws. Distances use base-2
logarithms. The native method selects representative bounds **among sampled
partitions inside the ball**, rather than searching all possible partitions:
the upper/lower vertical bounds have the fewest/most blocks, breaking ties
by greatest VI distance from $\hat z$; the horizontal bound is furthest away.
These are not a central credible interval for $K$.

```{r credible-ball, fig.height = 6}
cb <- credible_ball(sbm_fit, z_hat = z_hat, credible_mass = 0.95)
cb
plot_credible_ball(cb)
```

If the GitHub package `mcclust.ext` is installed,
`credible_ball(sbm_fit, z_hat = z_hat, method = "mcclust.ext")` provides a
cross-check using the reference implementation. Search and tie handling can
give different representative bounds; exact equality is not guaranteed.

### $\Pr(\theta_i > \theta_j \mid y)$ in the block model

```{r sbm-prob-stronger, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 8.5}
plot_prob_stronger(sbm_fit) +
  labs(title = expression(Pr(theta[i] > theta[j] ~ "|" ~ y)))
```

Shared block strengths create exact ties. In this tiered dataset, players
within a generating tier are usually *tied*
($\theta_i = \theta_j$), so both $\Pr(\theta_i > \theta_j \mid y)$ and
$\Pr(\theta_j > \theta_i \mid y)$ can be small. A small value alone does not
show that the row player is weaker: it can mean a tie. For distinct players,
these two probabilities and $\Pr(\theta_i=\theta_j\mid y)$ sum to one.
The tie probability is stored in the `prob_equal` attribute and equals the
posterior similarity (apart from the deliberately blank diagonal):

```{r sbm-ties}
p_sbm <- prob_stronger(sbm_fit)
round(attr(p_sbm, "prob_equal")[1:5, 1:5], 2)
```

### A second chain

```{r sbm-chain2}
sbm_fit2 <- fit_model(tennis_sbm, sbm_model,
  mcmc_control(iter = 10000, warmup = 5000, seed = 202))
full_join(
  posterior_K_table(sbm_fit) |> select(K, chain1 = probability),
  posterior_K_table(sbm_fit2) |> select(K, chain2 = probability), by = "K"
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Similar block-count distributions in independent chains are one useful (but
not sufficient) check of convergence.

# Dataset 2: the 2017 ATP season

The package includes head-to-head counts for the 105 top ATP players in each
season from 2000 to 2025.

## Explore the data

```{r atp-load}
atp <- ATP_2000_2025[["2017"]]
players <- atp$players_df
atp_data <- as_bt_data(atp$Y_ij, format = "matrix",
                       item_labels = make.unique(players$player_label))
atp_edges <- as_tibble(atp_data$wins, rownames = "winner") |>
  pivot_longer(-winner, names_to = "loser", values_to = "count") |>
  filter(winner != loser)
atp_data
```

```{r atp-eda}
atp_pairs <- atp_edges |>
  group_by(first = pmin(winner, loser), second = pmax(winner, loser)) |>
  summarise(matches = sum(count), .groups = "drop")
atp_overview <- tibble(
  players = atp_data$n_items, matches = sum(atp_edges$count),
  pairs_that_met = sum(atp_pairs$matches > 0),
  possible_pairs = nrow(atp_pairs)
)
atp_overview |> knitr::kable()
```

Unlike the synthetic league, most pairs never met: the data contain
`r atp_overview$matches` matches among `r atp_overview$players` players, covering
`r round(100 * atp_overview$pairs_that_met / atp_overview$possible_pairs, 1)`%
of possible pairs. The model links comparisons through common opponents.

```{r atp-eda-plots, fig.height = 4}
atp_players <- bind_rows(
  atp_edges |> transmute(player = winner, matches = count, wins = count),
  atp_edges |> transmute(player = loser, matches = count, wins = 0)
) |>
  group_by(player) |>
  summarise(across(c(matches, wins), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(win_rate = wins / matches) |>
  left_join(tibble(player = atp_data$item_labels, last_rank = players$last_rank), by = "player")
ggplot(atp_players, aes(matches)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#0072B2", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Matches against other top-105 players", y = "Players") + theme_minimal()
ggplot(atp_players, aes(last_rank, win_rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = matches), alpha = 0.6, colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Last observed ATP ranking in 2017 (log scale)", y = "Win rate", size = "Matches") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Win rate falls with ranking, but noisily, especially for players with few
matches.

## Fit the BT--SBM

```{r atp-fit}
atp_fit <- fit_model(
  atp_data,
  bt_sbm_model(shape_lambda = 2,
               item_clustering = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5)),
  mcmc_control(iter = 6000, warmup = 3000, seed = 1)
)
posterior_K_table(atp_fit)
```

The number of tiers is much less certain than in the synthetic league.

```{r atp-zhat}
set.seed(200)  # Reproduce the partition search.
atp_z <- partition_point_estimate(atp_fit)
table(atp_z)
names(atp_z)[atp_z == 1]          # the top tier
```

```{r atp-adjacency, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 9}
plot_ordered_adjacency(atp_fit, z_hat = atp_z, clean_fun = NULL)
```

Do the estimated tiers agree with the official rankings?

```{r atp-vs-ranking, fig.height = 4}
set.seed(201) # Reproduce the horizontal jitter.
atp_players <- atp_players |>
  left_join(tibble(player = names(atp_z), block = unname(atp_z)), by = "player") |>
  mutate(block = factor(block))
ggplot(atp_players, aes(block, last_rank)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Estimated block (1 = strongest)", y = "Last observed ATP ranking in 2017 (log)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Uncertainty about the tiers

```{r atp-cb}
atp_cb <- credible_ball(atp_fit, z_hat = atp_z)
atp_cb
atp_stability <- block_stability(atp_fit, atp_z)
atp_stability[, c("block", "size", "together", "split", "merged")]
```

The sampled bounds of this 95% VI ball have
`r atp_cb$n_blocks[["upper_vertical"]]` to
`r atp_cb$n_blocks[["lower_vertical"]]` blocks; this is not a 95% interval
for $K$. The table reports how often each estimated block is reproduced,
split or merged. The strongest estimated block is reproduced exactly in
`r round(100 * atp_stability$together[1], 1)`% of retained draws; it is split
in `r round(100 * atp_stability$split[1], 1)`% and merged with outside players
in `r round(100 * atp_stability$merged[1], 1)`%. Exact recovery of a block is a
stricter event than two specified players remaining together.

Membership probabilities for the most probable number of blocks:

```{r atp-assign, fig.height = 14, fig.width = 7}
plot_assignment_probabilities(atp_fit, clean_fun = NULL)
```

## Who is stronger than whom among the top players?

```{r atp-prob-stronger, fig.height = 7.5, fig.width = 8.5}
p_atp <- prob_stronger(atp_fit)
atp_equal <- attr(p_atp, "prob_equal")
federer <- grep("Federer", rownames(p_atp), value = TRUE)
nadal <- grep("Nadal", rownames(p_atp), value = TRUE)
plot_prob_stronger(atp_fit, max_items = 15) +
  labs(title = expression(Pr(theta[i] > theta[j] ~ "|" ~ y)))
```

Federer and Nadal share a block in
`r round(100 * atp_equal[federer, nadal], 1)`% of retained draws. This pairwise
tie frequency can be high even if the estimated top block is rarely reproduced
exactly, because other players can join them. Low strict-ordering probabilities
can reflect ties, so use `prob_equal` alongside `prob_stronger()`. The displayed
15 players are selected by posterior mean normalised strength, not by their
ATP ranking. The metadata field `last_rank` is the last ranking snapshot
available for each player in 2017, not necessarily a common year-end date.

# PL practical: ranked observations

This practical follows the PL theory session.

Rankings record items in order of preference rather than pairwise outcomes.
The Plackett--Luce (PL) model chooses the first item with probability
proportional to its strength, then the second among those remaining, and so on.
We use strict top-five rankings of ten sushi types. `sushi_toy()` is synthetic
and generates two preference profiles; it contains no original Sushi Preference
Dataset responses. For a first analysis we deliberately fit a single common
PL strength vector. This is a pooled model and does not represent the two
profiles; mixtures are available for that extension.

```{r pl-data, fig.height = 5}
sushi <- sushi_toy(n_rankings = 40, rank_length = 5, seed = 3)
sushi
head(sushi$rankings, 3)
plot_ranking_positions(sushi)
```

```{r pl-fit}
pl_fit <- fit_model(sushi, pl_model(shape_lambda = 1),
                    mcmc_control(iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, seed = 4))
summary(pl_fit)
```

As for BT, reported strengths are shares of total strength in each draw.

```{r pl-strength, fig.height = 5}
plot_strength_summary(pl_fit)
```

```{r pl-prob-stronger, fig.height = 6.5, fig.width = 8}
plot_prob_stronger(pl_fit)
```

The same `fit_model()` call also fits PL models with item blocks
(`pl_sbm_model()`), groups of ranking rows (`pl_mixture_model()`) or both
(`pl_lbm_model()`); see `vignette("pl-ranking-models", package = "RBBayes")`.

# MCMC run settings

The examples use different run lengths. This table separates total iterations,
discarded burn-in and retained draws; no thinning is applied. These settings
illustrate the workflow rather than establish that every posterior summary
has adequate effective sample size.

```{r run-settings}
fits <- list(BT = bt_fit, BT_SBM_1 = sbm_fit, BT_SBM_2 = sbm_fit2,
             ATP_BT_SBM = atp_fit, PL = pl_fit)
if (has_coda) fits <- append(fits, list(BT_2 = bt_fit2), after = 1)
run_settings <- bind_rows(lapply(names(fits), function(name) {
  fit <- fits[[name]]
  tibble(model = name, iterations = fit$control$iter, burn_in = fit$control$warmup,
         retained = nrow(as.matrix(fit)), seed = fit$control$seed)
}))
knitr::kable(run_settings)
```

# Exercises

1. Repeat `simulate_data(model = "bt-sbm")` with
   `latent_strength = c(12, 9, 2, 1)`. How do
   the posterior of $K$ and the credible ball change? What does
   `block_stability()` now report?
2. Repeat that block-model example with `matches_per_pair = 5`. Which summaries change most?
3. Refit the ATP season with `gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.8)` and with
   `dirichlet_process_prior(concentration = 1)`. Compare `prior_mean_K()` and
   `posterior_K_table()` for the two priors.
4. Choose another ATP season (e.g. `"2008"` or `"2023"`). Is the top tier
   larger or smaller than in 2017?

# Appendix: bayesplot diagnostics {#appendix-bayesplot}

These examples use the same normalised BT-strength draws as the coda section.
The trace plot shows two player parameters; the interval plot shows posterior
intervals for the four selected players. The appendix is skipped when
`bayesplot` is not installed and does not depend on `coda` being available.

```{r bt-bayesplot, eval = has_bayesplot, fig.height = 4}
top_players <- strength_summary(bt_fit) |>
  slice_head(n = 4) |>
  transmute(parameter = paste0("rel_strength[", item, "]")) |>
  pull(parameter)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(bt_fit, pars = top_players[1:2])
bayesplot::mcmc_intervals(bt_fit, pars = top_players, prob = 0.5, prob_outer = 0.95)
```
